utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-30-PT, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic, and Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann; I appear with my colleagues Mr. Keegan and Mr. Waidyaratne for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, Mr. President, I'm Krstan Simic, and I'm here on behalf of the first accused, Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, my name is Zarko Nikolic, and I'm the Defence counsel, together with Ms. Jelena Nikolic, I'm representing Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I'm Toma Fila and Vladimir Petrovic. I am here to represent Mladjo Radic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I'm Simo Tosic, defending Zoran Zigic. Lawyer Jelena Lopicic from Belgrade is not here, unfortunately, because her attendance here was not approved. I think this is wrong, because I believe that her attendance here should have been approved. My office is in Banja Luka, her office is in Belgrade, and in view of this and the state of war in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the communication between our two offices is very difficult, and for this reason we believe that in future, we should indeed be allowed to both be present at these sessions. Thank you. It would also be necessary, in the future, to be allowed to both attend Status Conferences and the trial. In all the other cases, legal counsel are allowed to attend all the sessions, and we see no reason why this should not be the same case in this particular instance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the matter looked into, Mr. Tosic, and if anything needs to be done, it will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a Status Conference. The items which I have for discussion are these: First of all, the status of disclosure; the status of witness protection; the requirements of the Rules for pre-trial briefs and the like; the amended indictment; the question of access to the shift statements from the police station; the status of inquiries into depositions; and finally any queries about detention. There is one other matter, which would be normally the question of setting date for trial. I have to tell you that this Trial Chamber is engaged in two cases, both substantial, and therefore, at the moment, it's not possible to fix a date for this trial. But arrangements in the Tribunal can never be fixed completely, and experience shows that there may be changes -- sometimes last-minute changes -- of plan, and for the moment, we will have in mind the necessity of starting this trial expeditiously, and we shall make every endeavour to find a date for it, but further than that, today, I can't go. And of course it's in connection with that that I made the original suggestion about depositions. Could we begin by matters of disclosure? I should say if there's anything else that anybody wishes to raise, of course, there will be opportunity to do so. But these are the matters which the Trial Chamber has in mind. And perhaps, Mr. Niemann, you could begin on that, dealing first of all with the witness statements and confirming, if you would, that they have been disclosed in Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Our position at the moment is that we have progressively disclosed all of the statements that we would foresee as being witnesses in the case, as well as statements of witnesses who may be available to the Defence under Rules such as Rule 68. There are still a number of documents which are to be translated, but we anticipate to be in a position to make them available, probably within the course of the next 14 days. Your Honours, just in relation to that, our position at the moment is that we are up to date in disclosing what material we believe we had used for trial. The only caveat we put on that is that, of course, as evidence comes to light, we may seek to either call additional witnesses or substitute witnesses. In the event that we do that, we will of course disclose it immediately that decision is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And in relation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In relation to the disclosure, could we detail the position about the disclosure of witness names? There have been problems in some cases where names haven't been disclosed, the intention being that pseudonyms will be obtained in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, pseudonyms, and in fact the witnesses were originally referred to by reference to numbers. The history of that, because it arose in the course of dealing with these depositions, Your Honour, I'll ask my colleague Mr. Keegan to outline the history of that, Your Honour, because he is more familiar with the dates and so forth in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thus far, as you have indicated, Your Honour, all of the witnesses' statements have been disclosed, given a number, and up to this date, only Mr. Fila's associate, with respect to the deposition motion, requested identification of the names that went with those numbers with respect to the witnesses that were proposed for depositions. We have prepared, however, a table, and it would be available after this session, at the end of the day, for disclosure, if it's necessary, if requested, of all of the names that go with the corresponding numbers, but obviously that would be a confidential document subject to the prior witness protection order of the Trial Chamber of -- I believe it's 18 December or 12 December, from that hearing we had. In addition, there are, of course, still certain witnesses who are the subject of protective measures, protective orders from prior trials, and so those witnesses we would intend to remain as pseudonymed witnesses, the letter pseudonyms, because of the prior rulings that protective orders continue in force unless otherwise ordered. So even on this list of numbered and named -- the table, certain witnesses, principally from the Tadic and Kovacevic trials, who were subject to protective orders would remain as pseudonymed witnesses until otherwise ordered. That would be our position at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But at some stage, presumably, the identifications and names will be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Upon request, we are prepared, as I said, to identify the names to all the statements other than those witnesses who are under existing protection orders from the prior trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it will be for you, presumably, to go back to those Chambers, insofar as it's possible, and get a release from those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Upon specific request, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if we make that request now, you could be starting with the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would seem to be sensible to deal with it as soon as possible, so that the Defence have the material, and to disclose your table today, any such disclosure subject to the usual confidentiality order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect to those pseudonymed witnesses, what we would prefer, I believe -- and Mr. Niemann may correct me on this, because obviously we hadn't talked about this completely -- but what we would prefer, if you will, is essentially to transfer those protective orders to this Trial Chamber for the time being, until such time when we can contact all of the witnesses to determine whether they wish to continue -- they would make the request to continue under those protective measures. We would then go through the process of requesting the same or similar protections for orders from this Trial Chamber, because those witnesses, obviously the burden was established of the necessity for protective measures in past trials. Those circumstances still exist, in our estimation. We would first need to confirm that with the witnesses, and then second, we would move before this Trial Chamber for similar protective measures. We would request the right to keep those names withheld until that process is concluded, and obviously we would move as expeditiously as possible in that regard, but we're only talking about, I think, eight or ten witnesses at the most. All of the rest of the names would be disclosed, subject to the existing protective measures that we have in this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what you propose is that you would disclose the table today; in regard to the eight to ten witnesses, you would ask that their names be withheld until you've had an opportunity of consulting with the particular witnesses, in which case you would apply to this Trial Chamber for protection? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Or, if the witness indicates that they no longer have the concerns which generated the protective measures in the first place, we'd simply move to cancel the prior orders and produce their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. How long do you want to do that? 28 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How many witnesses, in all, are we talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thus far, Your Honour, we have disclosed a total of 96 witness statements and/or transcripts. And with respect, your question about the provision of the translations in B/C/S, we in fact met with a couple of the Defence counsel yesterday. We are still awaiting a determination of whether the prior transcripts are in B/C/S; it's still not clear to us whether they have to be translated, and we're simply waiting for an answer from the records section on that. And then there were about, I think, eight statements, another eight statements that we're still awaiting the translations on. They have been submitted, and we just haven't got the translations. But except for those, all the rest have been provided in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Keegan, are you planning to call all those witnesses, all those whose statements you have provided by now, that is, 96 plus eight, which is 104? Are you planning to call all those witnesses here to appear before the Tribunal or will you make a distinction between those who will be making their depositions and those who will be called to testify here? This is the first question I have. And the second, have you estimated the time that you will need for those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It is our intention to try and stick to the original estimate of about 80 witnesses for the case for the Prosecution. What we can tell you today is which of those witnesses disclosed will comprise that final 80, because new witnesses are identified, and it will depend, of course, on the other matters, pre-trial matters, as they are decided in this case and the briefs and other things as the issues are flushed out, which of the witnesses are called for sure. The deposition witnesses is something that is on the agenda to be discussed, but we had prepared to -- we're obviously prepared to discuss that. If, for example, we take the Defence objections and simply follow those, in looking at our list, the list is down to about 18 witnesses that would be potentially -- of that list that we provided originally, that would be possible to use depositions for. Even there, it may be, for example, that we decide that we don't need all of those 18, and depositions may be even smaller. We can discuss the more-detailed mechanics of the depositions relating to some of the other issues raised later, if you prefer. But our position now is, no, our intent would not be to call 96 or more than that. We're going to try to stick to the 80, which was the original estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to the depositions in due course. The next matter which I had was the requirements of 73 bis. The Prosecution pre-trial brief has been filed, and I take it that everybody has that. Dealing with the other matters in the Rule, dealing with admissions and contested matters of fact and law and exhibits, perhaps the Prosecution can tell us what their position is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with relation to admissions of the parties and statements of contested matters of fact and law, for the Prosecution this becomes a bit of a guessing game as to what that is, because it really is for the Defence to indicate to us whether there are any matters which are not in dispute. In relation to statement of contested matters of fact and law, we're generally confronted with the situation that all matters are contested, unless advised otherwise. So I'm afraid that it's difficult for us to indicate much in terms of what we would perceive as the matters that are going to be contested and matters which aren't, save and except perhaps any questions of fact which have been resolved through the process of the adjudicated facts motion, and Your Honours have ruled on that. Insofar as those matters have been resolved, one could say that there is agreement on that. But save and except that, Your Honours, we're not in a position to indicate anything. But we do invite, certainly, the Defence to communicate with us, either through Your Honours or directly with us, on such matters, and we would be happy to entertain discussions in relation to those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps while you're on your feet, you could deal, please, with number 4, which concerns the witnesses you intend to call, and a summary of facts on which each will testify, and an estimate of the length of time. Are those matters in hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we had expected or anticipated that orders may be made today in relation to those matters, and we would expect to be required to provide that at some stage prior to the commencement of the trial, and we anticipate such an order. I don't know whether Your Honours require us to summarise the facts in relation to the witnesses, having regard to the fact there has been disclosure, but no doubt that could be attended to if that was considered necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall make orders in relation to the witnesses, the summaries, the points to which each will testify and the estimated length of time, the Prosecution to serve in two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that in two months of the commencement of the trial, Your Honours, may I enquire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's two months as of now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Niemann, I should simply like to remind you concerning the summaries. The Chamber is not waiting for the summaries for purely informal reasons, because we've had some unfortunate experience with summaries which did not serve any purpose, I mean summaries which said that there is such person who was at such and such place and he met another so and so at some other place, and it could apply to anything or anyone, so that I should like to insist in this particular case that these summaries are made with the strict view of helping the Chamber to get directly to the point about which the whole testimony is about so as to enable us to arrive at the truth. That is, we should learn from the summary which are different points which can be singled out from each and every testimony, and we also want to have a general summary which would represent a synthesis from which we could glean the strategy and what you're trying to draw out of all those different summaries. So this is very important. I mean a summary, as such, is not important. What is important is what is in it, and will you please always bear in mind that one needs to serve the course for which we are all here, and that is the course of truth, and thus these summaries should help us to immediately see what is it that one needs to focus in that particular case and to help us arrive at the truth in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can advise Your Honours that you can be rest assured that we will do everything we can to assist the Chamber, and indeed we see that as our duty. My concern about what Your Honours requested is that this becomes a bigger undertaking than just providing a short assessment of what each witness is going to say if one is to go into such things as analyses, which is normally one of the matters that I would have attended to in the course of my opening address. My concern, Your Honours, is that we believe that it would be preferable to give the details of these summaries and the order of witnesses and so forth at a time close to the commencement of trial, lest we be in a position where we would be seeking to perhaps not call certain witnesses and wanting to make variations when we get to the trial itself. This is complicated by the fact that we don't know at this stage which witnesses will be taken by depositions and which witnesses will be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I think we've got that in mind, but the problem is that we can't fix a date for trial. It's easier to deal with these matters if one can. So it would seem sensible to try and prepare as much as possible with, of course, it being kept in mind that nobody can foresee precisely what's going to happen. No one is going to hold you to the witnesses who you put forward if there are changes of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, Judge Bennouna raises the point as to whether you want more time to prepare than two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the point I make is that if the trial is not likely to be, having regard to the deposition process, if that goes ahead, the trial is not likely to be some considerable time down the track, it would certainly -- the more time we can have, the better product we can produce to satisfy the requirements as outlined by Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll say three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I turn next to the Defence. The Trial Chamber, under Rule 73 bis, may order the Defence at a Pre-Trial Conference to file a statement of admitted facts and law and a pre-trial brief addressing the factual and legal issues not later than seven days prior to the date set for trial. We would have in mind making orders of that sort. Again, we recognise that, of course, we are dealing with a case where we don't have a set date for trial, but the earlier it may be that the issues are clarified, the better it is for all of us. Is there any reason why we should not order a filing from each defendant on the admitted facts and law and a pre-trial brief addressing the factual and legal issues, so in answer to the Prosecution pre-trial brief, in three months? Is there any opposition to such a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The Defence has no objections, and we will accept your suggestions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I second my colleague, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, no objections to our making our submissions within the given deadline, both with respect to the brief and the facts. I am in an awkward situation to speak of things which I have not actually seen, because to date I have not received a copy of the amended indictment. What I wanted to say is we should make a certain distinction without trying to minimise the significance of any of the witnesses or among different facts, and in the spirit of speeding up the whole process, we would like to suggest that the Prosecution come up with a list of such witnesses, with full names and statements, which they intend to have examined outside of the trial so that we can get going, because we still don't know, out of these 98 statements, which witnesses it is that the Prosecutors actually are going to be calling here and which ones are going to be deposed somewhere else, and I don't know where that is going to be. So for me, this is a key issue at this Status Conference, because within this period of three months while we wait, we could use this time very well. We could reduce the number of these witnesses to a minimum. I proposed 14 witnesses which we can depose in this matter, and I have submitted the list. So for us, this is the key issue. Again, without trying to minimise the significance of these witnesses, they do not need any special protective measures, and I believe that my colleagues, Mr. Niemann and Keegan, will agree with this. We can right away determine where these witnesses are going to be examined, and we can come to a decision today. For those for which the Prosecution deems as necessary to be granted protective measures, within this period of three months we can find some time to deal with those. I believe that this is something that is acceptable for both parties and that would accelerate the whole process, because it has been 14 months since these accused have been detained, and there is obviously a new workload coming from my suffering country, and so I think we need to get going. Whatever the Prosecution had submitted to us, we have given our positions, what was acceptable and what was unacceptable to us, but I expect a certain amount of initiative on the part of the Prosecution to see what it is that we are actually coming with at trial, and we will give our positions. The Trial Chamber has ruled on the motions which we have submitted. There is a new indictment, an amended indictment. I am not going to make a pre-trial brief. I am just going to have the opening statement, and I'm going to reduce that, but I think that we need to do whatever we can so that we can come to the trial the best prepared. I think that we should really focus to only those witnesses who would testify to whether any of the accused has actually committed the crimes for which they are accused, in other words, whether they were in Omarska and what facts they know, and there will not be that many witnesses who will testify to that. This is my position, and I thank you for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the Defence of Zoran Zigic accepts in full the proposals of the Trial Chamber, and just for the economy of the trial, I think that we need to discuss where and when these witnesses who are in the territory of the Republika Srpska should be deposed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will come to the question of depositions shortly, but let me then make an order under 73 bis (F), ordering those matters within three months. Those are the matters I've already mentioned for the Defence to file. I want to turn just to deal with two other matters before we come to the depositions, and that is the amended indictment. If I didn't say so, three months to file the Defence documents. Moving to the amended indictment, does anybody want to make any submissions about that or time to make submissions? Anything you want to say about it? Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just only with respect to the issue Mr. Fila raised, that he hadn't received a copy yet, it appears that we were given inadvertently the wrong locker number, so it was put in the wrong locker downstairs for the Defence, and we were informed that he hadn't gotten it just before coming in here this afternoon, Your Honour. So that has been rectified, so it is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if there are any submissions, they should be made within 14 days. So if anybody for the Defence wants to raise anything in relation to the amended indictment, they can have 14 days. The next matter is the police station shift statements. The history of that matter is that the Prosecution have not been successful, as I recollect, have asked the Trial Chamber to raise the matter, and I take it we have done. I'll just ask the legal officer to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The formal request was made on the 29th of April, and we are awaiting a response from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, representatives from the Ministry of Justice of the Republika Srpska met with the Prosecutor in Sarajevo on the 8th of May, 1999, and said that the matter was in hand but it was very difficult to find the documents, despite every effort to do so, and that's the latest position with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I feel morally obliged, since I raised this issue, to show you -- I'm not sure who is supposed to be doing what. I have this document. It has been translated into English, but it only refers to the accused Radic. I can show it to the Prosecution, I can show it to you, because I told you the last time that I had seen it, and here it is. But the previous Defence counsel was given only a portion of it, which refers to Mladjo Radic. In other words, it was the other three accused were not covered. So what I have is going to explain the legal position of my client and perhaps Mr. Kos, and I can provide you with a copy of it whenever you want, if anybody questions the existence of this list. I can give you a letter which was -- a cover letter which came from the Ministry of Justice. If you wish, I can show it to you, a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date, Mr. Fila, of the letter from the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) 12 May '98, and it is in English, so you can actually review it. The original in Serbo-Croatian is in my hands, but I have a copy of the translation. So the usher could probably assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could hand it in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Of course. This is a copy, and the original is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) My apologies, Your Honours. Here are these long pieces of paper with stamps, but we couldn't copy them properly, so it was done with two copies each, and I can show you the original, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could we know if other Defence counsel, other Defence lawyers, have made similar moves to obtain these documents or not? Have other legal counsel made the same steps to obtain those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, this is what happened. Mr. Guberina, who was Defence counsel for Mr. Radic before me, had asked for it, and this was provided to him. So I sort of inherited it, I reviewed it, and I was told that I could not get it for other accused and for other Defence counsel because it was confidential, that I could only get it for my own client. I asked about it after the session here. I don't know what happened since. There may have been difficulties. But my colleague who preceded me had received it. And there are names of people who provided this list who state it there. And the best proof that this is an authentic document is that it does not suit me very well. Mr. Radic and I were wrong, but it suits other of the defendants. That is the assistance that I can provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be sensible for this document to be disclosed to the Prosecution, and then -- and other Defence counsel? If they want to pursue the matter further, it can be pursued; or otherwise, if this is sufficient, then there is no need to take the matter any further. I think it's simplest to be left to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I had an opportunity to see this ledger. This is a log, and after your suggestion, I tried to get the book and was told that the book has been lost. I think that this is information provided to the Prosecution on the 31st. However, today, I saw that this is an authentic excerpt from this logbook, with only the times of beginning and end of shift. Since that time, the logbook has been lost. All it is is a logbook which has noted the times of when certain individual officers came to work and left. There is also a witness on my witness list who compiled these logs, and I think that these persons shall be able to provide further clarifications of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We won't take that matter any further at the moment. We come now to the question of depositions. The original suggestion came from the Trial Chamber, having regard to the need to try and expedite matters, and was a suggestion for the hearing, at least of some witnesses, by way of deposition. We invited the parties to respond, which they have done, but the result is not, frankly, very clear. The principle, I think, is accepted on the whole. The purpose would be to have the evidence taken by a presiding officer -- who, because of the pressure of work, could not be a Judge of this Trial Chamber, but would have to be a suitably qualified presiding officer appointed for the purpose -- that the evidence would be taken down -- recorded, rather, by way of a video recording; that the usual rules of the giving of evidence would apply; and it would mean that while the witness would not appear in person before the Trial Chamber, there would be a video recording of that person's evidence for the Trial Chamber to see and in that way receive the evidence. The advantage it has, obviously, in a case like this, where there is no certain date for starting, is that it enables some of the evidence, at least, to be taken in advance, and will therefore save time at the trial proper and use the time between now and the trial as well as can be done. The initial response from the Prosecution was a very large one; I don't know if they've had a chance of reconsidering their position. The response from the Defence is also rather varied. It does seem to me, although some counsel are still to respond, it is a matter which should proceed, if possible, by way of agreement between the parties, and I wondered if counsel had had an opportunity of discussing this matter recently while everyone's been in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we haven't fully discussed it. Some of the counsel only arrived last night, I believe. But if they're going to be here, we are certainly prepared to discuss it. As I indicated earlier, we have done some consideration of our list, just taking the Defence responses as gathered thus far, and their objections falling into two primary grounds: One, of -- they object if they're a direct witness, that is, say something directly about one of the named accused; and the issue of judicial economy. We have several proposals in mind with regards to where and how the depositions could be taken, should we get to that point, and we've contacted some of the witnesses -- for example, Judge Greve -- to determine her schedule, since she's now a judge of the European Court of Human Rights. We are prepared to discuss it in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How many witnesses would you now propose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry about this hopping up and down, Your Honour. Going on what the Defence has raised, their objections, we have come up with a new list of approximately 20 witnesses, but we wouldn't like that to be seen as absolute in terms. I mean, I think that the suggestion made by Your Honours that this matter be resolved by discussion is indeed the best way to go, and I think that with discussions between the parties, we may be able to expand from that if necessary. It seems that any evidence of any witnesses that are not directly related to the offences charged, in terms of eyewitnesses to events as such, we could try and deal with by this process, and we would endeavour to do that. But we have prepared a list, and taking into account the objections raised, we come up with a figure of some 20 witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So how would you propose that we go from here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think that from what I've been able to see with respect to the responses and so forth, there hasn't been raised any particular opposition to the process as such. The only opposition raised is in relation to which witnesses will be dealt with. We initially gave a very large number, really because we wanted to say that the position of the Prosecution was that, if necessary, we would be happy to deal with all of them by the process of deposition. Obviously that was affected by the reaction from the Defence. So, taking into account, that's how we come up with this figure. The process that we would see is that if the Chamber is minded to make such an order, that either Your Honours could indicate in general terms that evidence will be taken by deposition and that someone will be appointed as presiding officer, and then I think that the best approach from there on in is for us to meet with the presiding officer at some set time and then just proceed by working out the logistics, bearing in mind any constraints that the Chamber may wish to impose upon the parties in relation to this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I just wonder, as a matter of formality, whether we can make a general order in those terms. Having regard to 71(b), I suppose what we could do is say, in general terms, that we will make such an order, subject to the agreement of the parties; and in due course, the parties having agreed the matter, we could either formally make the order, with the witnesses' names on, or we could summon another Status Conference to resolve it, although I would hope we could do it, perhaps, without that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That may not be necessary, Your Honours. I think if Your Honours encouraged the parties to meet, we can do that and determine such things as witnesses and where statements will be taken and any other matters that may arise, perhaps with liberty of the parties to apply in the event that there would be some irresolvable dispute, which -- I can't imagine that's going to happen. The point, though, that I think is important is that at some early stage, the presiding officer be appointed and the presiding officer be authorised to call a meeting of the parties, because it seems to me that much of the matters which may be discussed would have to be settled under the supervision of the presiding officer. In terms of where witnesses are going to be taken, I don't imagine the presiding officer determining which witnesses -- that would be matter of the Chamber -- but I would imagine that places of taking depositions, times, and so forth, all of which are important when it comes to reaching agreement on these matters, would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, for the interpreters, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you would foresee an order, as it were, in these terms: Parties to discuss deposition evidence; to report within 28 days, or something of the sort; the Trial Chamber to appoint a presiding officer, 14 days, with a view to calling a meeting, and an order for depositions in something like six weeks? That sort of timing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That sort of timing, I think, would be very helpful, Your Honour, yes, and an order along that line would he helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll just speak to the legal officer before I call on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, let me just -- before calling on you, just say what at the moment we have in mind, which would be to suggest a meeting, while you're all in The Hague, with the Prosecution to start this matter, and that there should be an agreed list of witnesses submitted to the Trial Chamber within 28 days together with a note as to their whereabouts. The procedure we would suggest is that once we have that list, we will appoint a presiding officer and determine the best place for the depositions to be taken, having in mind that of course it will partly depend on where the presiding officer can actually sit. So there are a number of considerations, obviously, to be borne in mind before we can make the final order. Having said that, that is merely what we have in mind at the moment, and that is that you meet -- first, an important step is that the parties all meet together and you have a conference with the Prosecutor and try and work out between you which of the witnesses are suitable and which aren't and then report that to us. Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, that would be an excellent idea if we knew who those witnesses were going to be and what they would be testifying to. We still do not know which witnesses the Prosecution should like to examine through deposition, so I should like to hear from the Prosecutor's office the period of time within which they will propose the list of witnesses whose testimonies would be taken by deposition, and then to meet with them and only then -- that is, after that, we could discuss it with our clients, with the defendants, to see if they agree with that or not. That is one thing. The second thing, I suggested that the evidence be taken by deposition from 13 witnesses, and I have submitted this, and I have not yet received an answer to that. I even submitted their names, and I have not heard whether they agree with that or not. Before we hold a meeting, if it is to be fruitful, the Defence team, as such, should like to invite the Prosecutor's office to give us the list of witnesses whose testimony should be made through deposition. After that, we would also submit our list, the list of the witnesses that would also be questioned out of this Court in this manner, and then we would meet and agree. In principle, the Defence thought we should not be accepting depositions of those witnesses who would be asked to testify about specific crimes, because that is one thing. When it comes to general things, to character witnesses and things like that, then it doesn't really matter. So I'm really asking the Prosecution to write their proposals, disclose, of course, the names of those people, compile their list, and then we would meet -- that is, the Defence team would meet with the Prosecution's team, and then we shall say whether we consent or not to that list and what are the names that we consent to and which are not. Likewise, the Prosecution should also read the list of witnesses that we should like to question in this manner, and only then can we really sit down and discuss it. Also, our clients need to see those lists, and I do not really know what I'm talking about when it comes to witnesses, because I do not know either those statements or anything, and the accused have not yet received the indictment, to this day, for instance; not even in English, let alone in Serbian. So I think that it would be best if Mr. Niemann or Mr. Keegan read out the list of those 20, or 30, or whatever the number of people, tell us who they are, and then we shall tell them we agree about those 15 or those -- I don't know, 18 or 20, we accept all those 20, say. It can be done, and I think it would simplify matters. I believe Mr. Niemann could do it within seven days, and then we would take another seven days to answer their list, and within a fortnight's time you would already have our definite answer, what we can go along with and what we can't go along with. I think it's quite simple. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think we can do better than that. Is there any reason why the list of 20 names shouldn't be handed over now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We can hand over this list of 20 now, Your Honour; it is available. But as I say, I would have thought that a meeting initially would have been more fruitful, so that we could discuss just precisely what the objections were. I mean, this process is only going to function if the parties are in agreement; otherwise the thing won't function at all anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it matters what way you do it. I would suggest you have a meeting now and decide at least the procedure that you're going to follow, and from there I hope that you can make some progress this weekend, rather than having to go home and trying to do it all from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, that is not the problem. To begin with, we have not been given their statements; secondly, we do not have the indictments in a language we understand, nor have the accused. So the four of us would have to meet, talk, and agree about everything, and it can't be done in half an hour. It's simply impossible to do it, and we cannot assume the responsibility of doing something which our clients will not agree with. But I want to say that there is no dispute as to how their evidence will be given. That is evidently up to the Chamber to decide when, how, and whether it will be over there or some other place. The people we are proposing will all be heard in Banja Luka. Luka; that is our proposal, and that is the nearest place which is perhaps the most convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Fila, just one practical point of view. You are saying that you do not have the statements, and you therefore cannot know which witnesses we are talking about, because you do not have the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, then, but when you receive the amended indictment, these statements, the proposed list prepared by the Prosecution, and after you have received all that, how long will you need to go through all that? Of course, it is up to the Prosecution to tell us whether the statements can be attached to the list; and the amended indictment, you have already heard it was simply the question of a misidentified locker, so you can have it. But after you receive that, when do you think -- after you have received all this information, how long will it take for you to be able to give an answer, that is, when could a meeting be held?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, to begin with, the four of us will have to discuss the matter and agree on our decision, and then we will of course have to see it with them. But these statements must also contain the names of those people, who are these people, not number 8, or number 9, or X, Y, Z, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I thought the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) But if they hand those things over to us today, then we shall be ready by tomorrow. If we can get it today by 5.00, tomorrow at noon you will have our answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution have said that they have disclosed all the statements. Now, Mr. Keegan, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have disclosed all of the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say you haven't got the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But in whose locker are the statements, and are the names and the surnames in those statements? I do not know who those 20 are that you are proposing. I have not seen it yet. If there are those 20 with names and surnames, who are these persons? Who are these individuals? Those individuals have their first names and their last names, and if I get it in the Serbian language today by 5.00, you will have the answer tomorrow by noon, by 12.00. Faster than that, we can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the list of 20 was drawn up about an hour ago to satisfy the Defence objections. No, Mr. Fila hasn't got the list of 20; yes, he does have the statements. And we did say that we could make the list available to him and identify the numbers of the witness statements which correspond. But there are other issues that he is raising, too, which I don't think I can resolve by way of discussion. He seems to say that he needs time to consider the indictment before he can consider this issue, and there is the other issue which I thought a meeting of the parties would be useful, and that is that not all counsel are in the same position, as it were, in relation to this process. But it seems that time needs to be set aside. If Mr. Fila says he needs to consider the indictment, I don't know what the relationship is, but no doubt he has his reasons. But that seems to be another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, may I ask, how can I tell you which are the reasons for the consideration of something that I've never seen, and how long I will need to think about something that I have not seen? I don't know what the indictment says. I really don't know how much time I need to go through it. I haven't been given the names of those 20 individuals, and yet you want me to tell you how much time I need. I repeat, give me the names of those 20 individuals, give me the translated indictments, and you will have our answer tomorrow by 1.00, and disclosure, so all the Prosecution has to do is give it to us by midnight today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are there any other Defence submissions? You want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, and the Prosecution should also say what they think about our proposals and give us the statement. We have not heard from them whether they agree that these witnesses be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I want to hear from other Defence counsel. Now, let us go on. Yes. Mr. Simic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, we were very happy when we heard the suggestion of the Trial Chamber what to do to make the whole procedure more expeditious and save time and money. However, the idea which was voiced by the Trial Chamber was misinterpreted by the Prosecution, because Rule 71 is very specific in this manner, very precise. We expected that our learned friends from the Prosecutor's office would submit the names of witnesses and summaries of those witnesses and that we would be ready today. In this regard, we did respond to the request of the Prosecution. We submitted the list of 22 witnesses whose evidence -- who could give their evidence by deposition, and we said that they could all be grouped over several days, and that that would add to the efficiency of the trial. And yet, today, we seem to be discussing matters as if this were the first time that we were meeting. And we really should very much like that time which we have until the beginning of the trial, to use this time as best we can. Thus, Mr. Kvocka's Defence has submitted a list of witnesses, the circumstances about which they should testify, and everything else, by complying with the suggestions made by the Trial Chamber. I don't think we do not have to go again into a repeat sterile discussion that would not yield any result. We expected the Prosecution to tell us today which ones of the witnesses proposed by our Defence, by Mr. Kos's Defence, by Mr. Radic's Defence, which ones of them they find acceptable and which ones they do not, but we have not yet heard their answer. So we still have those 22 witnesses or 21 witnesses, and we are expecting the Prosecution to comply with their obligation in accordance with Rule 71 to submit the list of their witnesses to see who might be giving their evidence by deposition and to give us -- to disclose the names and all the other things that they are under obligation to do. But I'm afraid that all this discussion will again take us nowhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm surprised that nobody seems to think it sensible that the parties should meet and discuss these matters round a table rather than making submissions to this Trial Chamber. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I shall try to avoid any repetition, but all these things that we are considering today, I shall try to use an illustration. At the Status Conference held last September, Mr. Niemann told you that the Prosecutor's office was planning to call 75 witnesses to testify before the Court and that they would need eight weeks. It is page 27 of the transcript, 3 to 11. You then issued the order, and the Defence was handed over the list of witnesses who would testify under Rule 71. This is the list, but here we have only the names of witnesses and the states or countries that they are in at present, and yet under Schedule D we were also to be handed over the statements of those witnesses. Mr. Keegan said that only Mr. Fila's office was disclosed the names. The Defence of the accused Kos was in touch with them and learned that it wasn't 24 witnesses but 23 witnesses, because Senad Cirkic and another one are identified under Number 2; that is, two persons under one and the same number. We studied the statements of 23 witnesses, and we made our submission in answer to the Prosecution's proposal. We have no objection, and I also would like to ask, if the Prosecution can do it while we are still here, could we be given this? Now it's come down to 20 witnesses, because out of 73, we've come down to 20 witnesses. Could the Prosecution give us at that meeting both the list and the statements? If it can be done today, as Mr. Fila said, we shall all do it overnight. We shall also have the opportunity of talking to our clients in the detention unit, but we shall be able to see what these statements say and then give our consent. I mean, we really don't feel -- we're really loath of writing new submissions, or new motions, or whatever, but today, if it could be done today, then we can study all those documents, discuss them with our clients, and have it all over and done with by tomorrow noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, will you be in The Hague tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Mr. Nikolic's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honours, I shall be in The Hague tomorrow, and I shall be here on Saturday. All the Defence counsel will be here. We are all going back on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if therefore we ordered you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "What about the meeting," somebody is saying, but the interpreter doesn't know who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please do not interrupt, because interpreting makes it very much more difficult. Now, if we were to direct you, the parties, counsel, to have a meeting in the next 24 hours or so, is there any reason why you should not be able to attend such a meeting with a view to moving things along?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, absolutely no reason why we couldn't do that at all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, to save time, I shall avoid repetition. I fully endorse all that my colleagues have already said, but all the material needs to be handed over to us. We do not have the indictment, we do not have witness statements in Serbian, and the Defence cannot go through those documents, nor can we discuss them with our clients. So we really need to see those documents today. As for the meeting, there should be no problem at all, because we are all here until Sunday, and we can meet with the Prosecution any time, provided that all these statements are handed over to us today in the Serbian language, because we simply have no other possibility of going through them, either we, as counsel for the Defence, or our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I do not understand this point about the statements. Now, you say you've disclosed them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think what we're talking about is the issue of the statements were originally disclosed only with the number, the coded number, and when this product was issued, it was issued with names. The Defence to this point haven't been given the full list of corresponding numbers to the names. That, I think, is the issue they are dealing with. That is what we will provide today at the close of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, if that's the issue. The orders that we make are that counsel are to meet within 24 hours to clarify the issues as to the taking of depositions, within 28 days to agree to a list of witnesses for whom depositions are to be taken, and to report to the Trial Chamber, together with a note as to the whereabouts of the witnesses. In that way, I hope it will be possible for the Trial Chamber to make suitable orders, having appointed a reporting officer for the taking of depositions in the not-too-distant future. But I do stress that these are matters which very much depend on the cooperation of the parties in order to achieve the goal that we've set ourselves. The other matter concerns the conditions of detention, and I'll ask the legal officer to remind me of the relevant Rule, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Rule 65 bis, which covers this conference, I notice has as one of its purposes to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure expeditious preparation for trial. It also requires the Chamber to review the status of the case and to allow the accused the opportunity to raise issues thereto, including the mental and physical condition of the accused. Now, does any counsel wish to raise any matter in relation to that? Do any of the accused want to raise anything? Very well. We'll adjourn the matter, save to say this, that we ought formally to fix another date, which we do. There may well have to be an earlier conference and, as I said, that we have in mind the necessity of fixing a date for trial in this case as early as possible. But meanwhile, we wish to ensure that depositions are taken. The conference should take place in the week commencing the 27th of September. If that is a Monday, that may be as suitable a day as any. Is that a Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 2.30 that day. We'll adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of September, 1999, at 2.30 p.m.
